lessons.title: 黒字でも廃業する理由：後継者問題の全体像
lessons.body:
日本では毎年、倒産していないのに事業をやめる会社が数万社あり、そのおよそ半分は黒字でした。経営者が高齢になり、引き継ぐ人が決まっていないためです。このレッスンでは、その規模、測り方、そして酒蔵と工芸で特に深刻な理由を整理します。

### 3つの数字は別々のものを測っている

よく引用される統計が3つあり、混同されがちです。

| 指標 | 最新の数字 | 何を数えているか |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 後継者不在率 | 2025年 50.1% | 後継者が「いない」または「未定」と答えた企業の割合。[帝国データバンク](https://www.zaikei.co.jp/releases/3194399/)、約27万社が対象 |
| 休廃業・解散 | 2025年 6万7,210件 | 倒産ではなく、自主的に事業をやめた企業の数。[東京商工リサーチ](https://www.tsr-net.co.jp/data/detail/1202284_1527.html) |
| 後継者難倒産 | 2025年度 461件 | 後継者不在が一因となった倒産の数。[東京商工リサーチ](https://www.tsr-net.co.jp/data/detail/1202733_1527.html) |

最も重要なのは2番目です。休廃業・解散は後継者難倒産の100倍以上あります。損失の大半は目立たない形で起きています。事業がただ止まるのです。

### 逆説：不在率は改善しているのに、廃業は減らない

後継者不在率は7年連続で下がり、ピークだった2017年の66.5%から50.1%になりました。帝国データバンクは、官民の相談窓口が広がったことを理由に挙げています。

一方で、休廃業・解散は2025年に前年比7.2%増え、3年連続で過去最多でした。後継者難倒産も過去最多です。この2つが同時に起きているのは、準備をしてこなかった経営者がすでにかなりの高齢になっているからです。

- 2025年に休廃業・解散した企業のうち、代表者が60代以上だったのは90.6%。
- 80代以上は34.0%で、初めて30%を超えました（[ECのミカタ](https://ecnomikata.com/ecnews/49221/)、東京商工リサーチ調査の報道）。
- 後継者難倒産では、代表者の死亡と体調不良が原因の約85%を占めます。

つまり、準備を済ませた企業は増えたものの、準備しなかった企業には時間が残っていません。

### 黒字の会社もやめている

2025年に休廃業・解散した企業のうち、赤字だったのは47.2%でした。裏を返せば、半分強は黒字のままやめたことになります。買い手の立場から見て興味深いのはここです。顧客のいる事業が、需要とは関係のない理由で消えています。

### 誰が最も影響を受けているか

業種よりも、規模と地域の差が大きく出ます。

| 区分 | 後継者不在率（2025年） |
| --- | --- |
| 大企業 | 24.9% |
| 中小企業 | 51.2% |
| 小規模企業 | 57.3% |
| 三重県（全国最低） | 33.9% |
| 秋田県（全国最高） | 73.7% |

規模別の数字は、同じ調査を報じた[ITmediaの記事](https://www.itmedia.co.jp/business/spv/2601/07/news040.html)によります。三重県が低い理由として帝国データバンクは、地域金融機関の密着した支援と、商圏が安定していて同族内で引き継ぎやすい環境を挙げています。

### 警鐘はどう鳴らされたか

2017年、中小企業庁がその後10年の政策を方向づける試算を公表しました。2025年までに、平均引退年齢の70歳を超える中小企業・小規模事業者の経営者が約245万人になり、うち約127万人は後継者が未定だという内容です。放置すれば、10年間の累計で約650万人の雇用と約22兆円のGDPが失われる可能性があるとしました（[ニュースイッチ](https://newswitch.jp/p/10544)）。

これが「2025年問題」と呼ばれるようになりました。[大阪産業経済リサーチセンターの2025年の論考](https://www.pref.osaka.lg.jp/documents/33150/202502jigyosyokei.pdf)は、当初の想定ほど深刻にはならなかったとしつつ、後継者不在のまま70歳を超えた経営者は一定数残っており、その多くが経営状況にかかわらず廃業の意向を持っている可能性があると指摘しています。

### 親族承継は主流でなくなりつつある

かつては子ども、多くは息子が継ぐのが当たり前でした。帝国データバンクによると、新任社長では親族以外の社内人材の昇格が同族承継とほぼ並び、同社はこの流れを「脱ファミリー化」と呼んでいます。社外への売却はこの10年で増えましたが、2025年は割合がわずかに下がりました。

親族承継という前提がどれほど根深いか、それが崩れることがなぜ大きな転換なのかは、第2回で扱います。

### 酒蔵と工芸で特に深刻な理由

どちらも、担い手の高齢化、国内需要の縮小、習得に何年もかかる技能という3つが重なっています。

**酒蔵。** 清酒の出荷量は1973年度の177万キロリットルから、2023年度には39万キロリットルに減りました。清酒製造場の数は1989年の2,459場から2023年には1,562場になっています（[国税庁資料](https://www.chisou.go.jp/tiiki/kokusentoc_wg/r7/pdf/250521_shiryou_1_3.pdf)）。業界の偏りも大きく、大手50者が出荷量の68%を占める一方、小規模な1,089者は合わせて7%です。

酒蔵には特有のルールがあります。清酒の製造免許は新規には事実上交付されないため、参入するには既存の蔵を引き継ぐしかありません。譲渡案件もこの点をはっきり書いています。[長崎県の創業約200年の蔵の案件](https://batonz.jp/sell_cases/83179)は、免許を買い手が手に入れられる参入障壁として説明しています。上の国税庁資料はこの規制の緩和を扱ったもので、第12回で詳しく見ます。

**工芸。** 国指定の伝統的工芸品産業の従事者は、1974年の約28万人から2022年度には約4.8万人に減りました。生産額は1982年の約5,300億円から、2009年には約1,280億円になっています（[東京財団の資料](https://www.tkfd.or.jp/files/files/doc/file_No.1.pdf)）。現在の従事者の63.6%は50代以上で、70代以上は20代以下の3倍います（[文化庁の資料](https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkashingikai/bunkazai/kikaku/r07_r08/05/pdf/94408301_03.pdf)）。

### ビジネスとして見ると

以下は上の事実に基づく私の解釈で、出典のある主張ではありません。

1. **売りに出る事業は多く、今後も増える。** 80代の経営者による廃業が過去最多ということは、多くの会社が数年のうちに持ち主が変わるか、なくなるということです。
2. **安いことと良いことは別。** 私が見つけた酒蔵の譲渡案件は、ほとんどが赤字で借入を抱えていました。価値があるのは現在の商売ではなく、免許、屋号、建物であることが多いです。
3. **タイミングを決めるのは経営者の健康。** 倒産の大半が死亡や病気をきっかけに起きている以上、経営者がまだ教えられるうちに話を始めるほうが、はるかに価値があります。

### 重要用語

| 用語 | 英語 | 補足 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 事業承継 | business succession | このコース全体の主題 |
| 後継者不在 | no successor | 調査では「未定」も含む |
| 休廃業・解散 | closure or dissolution | 倒産ではなく自主的な撤退 |
| 黒字廃業 | closing while profitable | 最も問題視されている現象 |
| 親族内承継 | family succession | 従来の主流 |
| 第三者承継 | third-party succession | 社外への譲渡。多くはM&A |

lessons.title: 「家」と跡取り：1945年以前の承継
lessons.body:
1945年以前の日本では、事業は個人のものではなく「家」のものでした。家の財産と地位は一人の跡取りがまとめて受け継ぎ、ふさわしい息子がいなければ、成人を養子や婿として迎えて跡取りにしました。この仕組みが、日本に100年以上続く会社が多い理由の一つであり、同時に「子が継ぐのが当たり前」という前提の出どころでもあります。このレッスンでは、家督相続、婿養子、商家の組織の3つを順に見ます。

### 「家」とは何だったか

ここでいう「家」は、血縁の家族そのものではなく、名前、財産、家業をひとまとまりにして代々引き継ぐ単位です。当主は家の財産を預かる管理者で、自分の代で家をつぶさずに次へ渡すことが役目とされました。

[Mehrotra、Morck、沈、Wiwattanakantangの論文](https://randallmorck.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/13-adoptive-expectations-rising-sons-in-japanese-family-firms.pdf)は、江戸時代の法のもとで家は分割せずに一人の男子の跡取りへ渡す必要があったと説明しています。財産を兄弟で分けると、家業の規模が代を追うごとに小さくなります。それを避けるための単独相続でした。

### 家督相続：一人がすべてを継ぐ

家督相続とは、戸主（家の長）の身分と財産を一人の相続人がまとめて引き継ぐことです（[コトバンク「家督相続」](https://kotobank.jp/word/家督相続)）。

1. **起源。** 武家では室町時代中期以降に長子相続が発達し、江戸時代に家督相続として制度化されました。この慣行は百姓や町人にも広がりました。
2. **法律化。** 1898年（明治31年）公布の民法（明治民法）で全国一律の制度になりました。相続の順位は直系卑属（子や孫）が先で、男子が女子より、年長者が年少者より優先されたため、普通は長男が継ぎました。
3. **隠居。** 当主が生きているうちに家督を譲ることを隠居といい、明治民法では原則として満60歳以上が条件でした（[コトバンク「隠居」](https://kotobank.jp/word/隠居)）。江戸時代の町人の間では、早めに引退して気ままに暮らす「楽隠居」が理想とされました。
4. **廃止。** 1947年の民法改正で、家督相続も隠居も廃止されました。

つまり戦前の経営者は、引退の時期も後継者も、家の制度の中で自然に決まっていました。第1回で見た「準備をしないまま高齢になる経営者」は、この仕組みがなくなった後に生まれた問題だといえます。

### 婿養子：跡取りを「選ぶ」仕組み

長男が継ぐのが原則でしたが、実際には養子がよく使われました。息子がいない場合だけでなく、息子に能力が足りない場合にも、外から有能な人を迎えたのです。

- **婿養子。** 娘の夫を養子として迎え、家の名前と跡取りの地位を継がせる形です。婿は生家の名前を捨てて妻の家に入ります（上記論文）。
- **商家での使い方。** 江戸時代の商家は、優秀な奉公人に娘を嫁がせたり、養子にしたりして報いることがありました。大阪・船場の商人の一部には、娘が生まれると赤飯を炊いて祝う習慣があったとされます（[沈政郁「日本の家族企業の事業承継戦略」](https://www.kyoto-su.ac.jp/project/kikou/sekaimondai/kenkyu/pdf/20150105_kenkyu03.pdf)）。息子は選べませんが、娘の婿は選べるからです。
- **成人養子が中心。** 日本の養子縁組の大半は成人です。司法統計年報によれば、2004年の養子縁組8万3,505件のうち成年は8万2,175件でした（同資料）。上記論文は1990年以降、成年の割合が97〜98%で推移していると述べています。

この慣行は戦後も上場企業で続きました。上記論文は1962〜2000年の上場企業1,367社を分析し、婿や養子など血縁でない跡取りが率いる会社は、実の息子が率いる会社より総資産利益率（ROA）が約0.56ポイント高く、創業者が率いる会社と統計的に差がないことを示しました。著者たちは、実の息子が養子に地位を奪われうることが、息子自身の努力も促したと解釈しています。

### 商家の組織：家と経営を分ける

大きな商家は、家族だけでは回せないため、奉公人の階層と、家の財産を守るルールを作りました。

| 仕組み | 中身 | 承継上の意味 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 奉公人の昇進 | 丁稚から手代、番頭へと昇進する。番頭は使用人の最高位で、30歳前後で勝ち抜いた者がなったとされる（[大阪市中央区の資料](https://www.city.osaka.lg.jp/chuo/cmsfiles/contents/0000508/508145/8ura.pdf)） | 当主が若くても、経験ある番頭が実務を支えた |
| 暖簾分け | 長年勤めた奉公人が「別家」として独立し、主家の屋号の使用や得意先・販売圏の分与を受ける。同じ商売を禁じられることもあった（[コトバンク「暖簾分け」](https://kotobank.jp/word/暖簾分け)） | 有能な人材をつなぎとめ、本家を中心にした同族のネットワークを作った |
| 家産の共有 | 三井家は1710年に京都に「大元方」を置いて家政と事業を一元的に統轄し、1722年の「宗竺遺書」で遺産を分割せず同族9家で共有する形を固めた（[コトバンク「三井家」](https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E4%BA%95%E5%AE%B6-138812)） | 一人の当主の失敗や分家で事業が割れるのを防いだ |

### 老舗という結果

こうした仕組みの結果として、日本には長寿企業が多く残りました。帝国データバンクによると、2025年12月時点で業歴100年を超える老舗企業は4万6,708社です（[帝国データバンク調査の配信](https://www.zaikei.co.jp/releases/3365307/)）。細かい業種で見ると、清酒製造業は老舗が938社あり、業種内で老舗が占める割合は91.9%と全業種で最も高い値です。酒蔵の多くは、ここで見た家の仕組みで代々続いてきた会社だということです。

最古とされる金剛組（578年創業の寺社建築会社）も、息子がいない代には婿が金剛の姓を名乗って継いだとされます（[Wikipedia英語版](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong%C5%8D_Gumi)）。それでも金剛家による経営はバブル崩壊後の負債で行き詰まり、同業の髙松建設の傘下に入りました。その時期は[nippon.com](https://www.nippon.com/hk/japan-topics/g00702/)が2005年、Wikipediaが2006年1月（事業譲受の時点）としており、代数も前者が41代、後者が40代と食い違います。ここでは両方を併記します。家の仕組みは長く続きますが、それだけで経営の失敗を防げるわけではない例です。

### 戦後の制度とのずれ

家督相続が廃止された後、子どもたちは原則として平等に相続する権利を持ち、一定の取り分（遺留分）も保障されるようになりました。会社の株を後継者一人に集めても、他の相続人が遺留分を主張すると株が分散するおそれがあります。この問題に対応するため、2008年施行の経営承継円滑化法に、遺留分の計算から自社株を外す「除外合意」などの特例が設けられました（[BUSINESS LAWYERS](https://www.businesslawyers.jp/practices/17)）。お金と税金の論点は第7回で扱います。

### ビジネスとして見ると

以下は上の事実に基づく私の解釈で、出典のある主張ではありません。

1. **「外から迎える」は日本の伝統の一部。** 婿養子や暖簾分けは、血縁外の人に家業を託す古い方法でした。第三者承継を「家業の終わり」と見る経営者には、この歴史が説得の材料になりえます。
2. **老舗が売っているのは名前と信用。** 酒蔵の譲渡で屋号や銘柄が重視されるのは、家が何代もかけて守ってきたのがまさにそれだからです。買い手は、それを守る役目も一緒に引き受けることになります。
3. **番頭の不在が今の弱点。** かつての商家には当主を支える番頭がいました。今の小さな会社は社長一人に知識が集中しがちで、それが承継を難しくしています。

### 重要用語

| 用語 | 英語 | 補足 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 家（いえ） | ie, the household as a continuing unit | 名前・財産・家業を代々引き継ぐ単位 |
| 家督相続 | headship succession (single-heir inheritance) | 1898年に法制化、1947年に廃止 |
| 戸主 | head of household | 家督相続で継がれる地位 |
| 隠居 | retirement of the household head | 明治民法では原則60歳以上 |
| 婿養子 | adopted son-in-law (mukoyoshi) | 娘の夫を養子にして跡取りにする |
| 番頭 | head clerk | 商家の使用人の最高位 |
| 暖簾分け | noren-wake (licensed spin-off by a former employee) | 屋号の使用や得意先の分与を伴う独立 |
| 遺留分 | legally reserved share of inheritance | 現在の承継で株が分散する原因の一つ |

lessons.title: 戦後の創業者世代と後継者不足の始まり
lessons.body:
日本の中小企業の経営者は、ある時期にほぼ一つの世代で占められていました。高度成長期に事業を起こしたり継いだりした人たちが、交代しないまま年を重ね、2010年代半ばにはそろって60代後半に達しました。このレッスンでは、その世代がなぜ生まれ、なぜ席を譲らなかったのか、そして「2025年問題」とは何を指していたのかを整理します。

### 経営者の年齢の山が動いた

経営者を年齢ごとに数えると、最も人数の多い年齢（ピーク）があります。このピークが20年でほぼ20歳ずれました。

| 時点 | 最も多い年齢・年齢層 | 出典 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1995年 | 47歳 | [ニュースイッチ（日刊工業新聞）](https://newswitch.jp/p/7391) |
| 2000年 | 50〜54歳 | [2023年版中小企業白書](https://www.chusho.meti.go.jp/pamflet/hakusyo/2023/PDF/chusho/04Hakusyo_part2_chap2_web.pdf) |
| 2015年 | 66歳（65〜69歳） | 同上、ニュースイッチ |
| 2020年・2022年 | 60〜74歳に分散 | 2023年版中小企業白書 |

山が毎年ほぼ1歳ずつ右へ動いたということは、同じ人たちが経営者の席に座り続けたということです。[商工中金の講義資料](https://www7.econ.hit-u.ac.jp/shokochukin/archives/2016/20160608_01.pdf)（2014年版中小企業白書のデータ）は、2015年時点のボリュームゾーン（最も人数が多い層）を66〜68歳の団塊の世代としています。

団塊の世代とは、1947年から1949年の第1次ベビーブームに生まれた世代です。作家の堺屋太一が1976年の小説『団塊の世代』で使った言葉が広まりました（[コトバンク](https://kotobank.jp/word/団塊の世代)）。人数は辞典によって約689万人とも約810万人ともされ、一致しません。

### 戦後の創業ブームと、その世代（歴史）

第2回で見たとおり、1947年の民法改正で家督相続が廃止され、跡取りが自動的に決まる仕組みはなくなりました。翌1948年8月には、中小企業政策の専門官庁として中小企業庁が通商産業省の外局に置かれています（[アジア歴史資料センター](https://www.jacar.go.jp/exhibition/glossary/term1/0110-0010-0050-0040-0200.html)）。

その後の数十年は、会社が次々と生まれた時代でした。[ニッセイ基礎研究所の2004年のレポート](https://www.nli-research.co.jp/files/topics/36304_ext_18_0.pdf?site=nli)によると、開業率（既存の企業数に対する新規開業の割合）は1970年代ごろまで約6%で推移し、新規開業は年に約28万社ありました。それが80年代以降に下がり、90年代には開業率が廃業率を下回る「逆転」が続くようになります。

つまり、高度成長期からその後にかけて創業した人や家業を継いだ人が大きな層をつくり、その下の世代では新しく経営者になる人が減りました。人口の山と、創業の山が重なったのです。

### なぜ交代が進まなかったか

山がそのまま動いた直接の理由は、経営者が交代しなくなったことです。

1. **交代率の低下。** 経営者が交代した企業の割合は、昭和50年代（1975〜84年）の平均4.97%から、2000年以降は平均3.48%、2011年には2.46%まで下がりました（商工中金の講義資料）。
2. **平均年齢の上昇。** 同じ資料では、経営者の平均年齢は昭和50年代の52〜53歳から近年は59歳になっています。
3. **子が継がなくなった。** [中小企業庁の2006年の資料](https://www.chusho.meti.go.jp/zaimu/shoukei/2006/download/060927zigyou_shi1.pdf)が引く東京商工リサーチの2003年調査では、子息・子女への承継の割合は「20年以上前」の79.7%から「0〜4年前」の41.6%に下がり、親族以外への承継が6.4%から38%に増えています。

子が継がないのに、外部への承継の仕組み（第5回以降で扱う支援や市場）はまだ整っていませんでした。その間、経営者は自分で続けるしかなかったと考えられます。

### 「2025年問題」とは何だったか

「2025年問題」には2つの意味があり、混同されがちです。

- **社会保障の2025年問題。** 団塊の世代が2025年までに全員75歳以上の後期高齢者となり、医療・介護の給付が増えるという問題です（[第一生命経済研究所](https://www.dlri.co.jp/files/dlri/339772.pdf)）。
- **中小企業の2025年問題。** 中小企業庁が2017年に示した試算です。2025年までに平均引退年齢の70歳を超える経営者が約245万人、うち約127万人は後継者未定で、放置すれば10年間の累計で約650万人の雇用と約22兆円のGDPが失われうるとしました（[ニュースイッチ](https://newswitch.jp/p/10544)）。

後者の数字は予測ではなく、仮定の置き方に左右される試算です。70歳超の経営者の企業のうち、法人の31%、個人事業者の65%が廃業すると仮定しています（同記事）。第1回で見たとおり、実際には当初の想定ほど深刻にはならなかったという評価もあります。

この試算と前後して、国は承継の政策を一気に積み上げました（[中小企業庁の2021年の事務局資料](https://www.chusho.meti.go.jp/koukai/kenkyukai/jigyousyoukei_guideline/001/001_03.pdf)）。

| 年 | 施策 |
| --- | --- |
| 2006年 | 事業承継ガイドライン策定 |
| 2009年度 | 法人版事業承継税制の創設 |
| 2011年 | 事業引継ぎ支援センター設置（2016年に全国展開） |
| 2016年12月 | ガイドラインを10年ぶりに改訂 |
| 2017年度 | 事業承継診断の推進開始 |
| 2018年度 | 法人版事業承継税制の抜本拡充 |
| 2021年4月 | 事業承継・引継ぎ支援センターへ改組 |

### 2025年を過ぎた今

2023年版中小企業白書は、2020年以降は山が60〜74歳に分散し、団塊の世代の経営者の引退がうかがえる一方、75歳以上の割合は上がり続けていると指摘しました。承継を済ませた企業と、済ませていない企業の「二極化」です。

最新の社長年齢の調査は、調査会社によって数字がかなり違います。

| 調査 | 平均年齢 | 70代以上の割合 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [帝国データバンク](https://www.zaikei.co.jp/releases/3304434/)（2025年末） | 60.8歳（35年連続で最高） | 25.1%（70代19.5%、80代以上5.6%の合計） |
| [東京商工リサーチ](https://webtan.impress.co.jp/n/2026/03/12/52284)（2025年12月） | 63.81歳 | 34.79% |

差が出る主な理由は対象の範囲です。東京商工リサーチは約440万社のデータで、個人事業主や会長も「社長」に含めています。帝国データバンクの60.8歳は合資・合名会社の代表社員や理事長などを除いた数字で、それらを含む全法人では61.7歳です。このレッスンでは傾向を見るために両方を示しますが、小さな事業者の実態に近いのは対象の広い東京商工リサーチの数字だと考えます。統計の読み方は第4回で詳しく扱います。

経営者の意向も変わっていません。日本政策金融公庫の2023年の調査では、廃業を予定する企業が57.4%に上り、その理由で最も多いのは「そもそも誰かに継いでもらいたいと思っていない」（45.2%）でした（[日本政策金融公庫総合研究所](https://www.jfc.go.jp/n/findings/pdf/sme_findings230323.pdf)）。この調査は小規模な事業者が多く含まれる点に注意が必要です。

### ビジネスとして見ると

以下は上の事実に基づく私の解釈で、出典のある主張ではありません。

1. **案件の波はまだ終わっていない。** 山は分散しましたが、75歳以上の層は厚くなっています。急いで売る必要のある会社は、これからも出てきます。
2. **相手の年齢が交渉の前提を決める。** 70代後半の経営者は、引き継ぎ期間を長く取れません。買い手や後継者は、技術や取引先の引き継ぎを短期間で進める計画を最初から持つ必要があります。
3. **「継がせたくない」経営者が多い。** 半数近くが誰かに継いでもらうこと自体を考えていません。こうした経営者には、売却を勧めるより先に、事業が残ることの意味を話すほうが入口になりそうです。

| 事業承継診断 | succession readiness check | 2017年度から推進 |

lessons.title: Japan in Britain: the shape of the market
lessons.body:
Britain's appetite for Japan is at a record on every measure I could find: trips, restaurants and event attendance. This lesson sets out the three strands, how big each is, and who is making money from them. The short answer to the last question is that it is mostly not Japanese companies.

### Strand 1: travel

In 2025, 535,004 British visitors went to Japan, up 22.4% on the year before. It was the first time the figure passed half a million ([Honichi Lab](https://honichi.com/news/2026/03/16/inbound-uk-2025/), reporting Japan's tourism agency). The 2024 figure was about 437,000, itself a record.

They spend heavily. British visitors spent ¥207.6 billion in Japan in 2025, about ¥391,000 each. Every month of 2025 beat the same month of 2024, and April, with the Easter school holidays, was the strongest.

Three things are driving it.

- **The weak yen.** Japan is cheap for someone paid in pounds.
- **Social media.** A [BBC report in August](https://view.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2026090108584181613), relayed by Asia Economy, described a craze among younger Britons fed by travel videos.
- **More ways to fly.** Japan's tourism office in London has said about a fifth of British arrivals came on Chinese airlines, which are often cheaper, and that there is no direct London to Osaka flight ([Travel Weekly](https://travelweekly.co.uk/news/tourism/japan-continues-to-enjoy-soaring-demand-from-uk-market)).

Most first-time visitors follow the "Golden Route" of Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka. Japan's tourism agency wants them elsewhere, and in other seasons, to ease crowding.

### The flow has reversed

In the late twentieth century the typical traveller between the two countries was Japanese. That is no longer true. [VisitBritain](https://www.visitbritain.org/markets/japan) counted 226,000 visits from Japan to the UK in 2024 and forecasts 276,000 for 2026.

So more than twice as many Britons now go to Japan as Japanese come to Britain. A business built for Japanese tourists in London is serving the smaller flow. One built for Britons planning Japan is serving the larger one.

### Strand 2: food and drink

The research firm [IBISWorld](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-kingdom/market-research-reports/japanese-sushi-restaurants-industry) counts 2,834 Japanese and sushi restaurant businesses in the UK in 2026, with revenue of £1.6 billion. It says the number of businesses has grown 3.9% a year since 2021.

Treat any count with caution. Another data seller, [BoldData](https://companydata.com/uk/japanese-restaurants/), lists over 10,000 "Japanese restaurants", with 27% in London. The gap is one of definition: whether a takeaway that sells sushi alongside other food counts.

IBISWorld names three companies as the largest.

| Company | Founded | Founder | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Wagamama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagamama) | 1992, Bloomsbury | Alan Yau | The largest. 161 UK restaurants in 2024, with plans for 200 or more |
| [YO! Sushi](https://yo.co.uk/yo-sushi/) | 1997, Soho | Simon Woodroffe | Brought conveyor-belt sushi to Britain |
| Wasabi | 2003, London | Dong Hyun Kim | Sushi and bento chain. Founding details are from my own knowledge, not a source read this week |

None of the three was founded by a Japanese person or a Japanese company. [Zoom Japan](https://zoomjapan.info/2016/05/11/no41-restaurant-20-years-of-revolving-sushi-in-the-uk/) made the point directly: the chains that act as Britain's gateway to Japanese food were mostly started by non-Japanese founders. Wagamama's own description is "Japanese-inspired".

This is the most important structural fact about the food strand. The mass market was built by adaptation, and the Japanese-run businesses sit mainly at the two ends: specialist grocers and high-end restaurants.

### Strand 3: culture

Culture is the hardest strand to size, because it runs from anime and games to pottery classes. Two venues give a sense of scale.

- **Hyper Japan.** The festival began in 2010. It drew 53,000 visitors in 2025 ([JETRO listing](https://www.jetro.go.jp/en/database/j-messe/tradefair/detail/159501)) and has added a Manchester edition. The Japanese printing group Toppan [bought its organiser in 2024](https://ctiweb.co.jp/con/en/toppan-holdings-acquires-cross-media) to sell anime and manga merchandise through it.
- **Japan House London.** Opened by Japan's foreign ministry in 2018 on Kensington High Street. It had welcomed more than 2.2 million visitors by early 2025 ([Japan House report](https://www.japanhouse.jp/en/n_pdf/whatsjh/report/report_202503_en.pdf)).

One is commercial and one is state-funded. That split runs through the whole culture strand, and lesson 16 looks at it.

### How the strands feed each other

The three strands share customers. Someone who eats ramen weekly is more likely to book Tokyo, and someone back from Tokyo is fussier about ramen. [Nippon.com](https://www.nippon.com/en/features/h00218/number-of-overseas-japanese-restaurants-tops-100-000.html) reports the same effect worldwide: tourists returning from Japan drive demand for Japanese restaurants at home.

With over half a million Britons a year now visiting, the number of people who know what the real thing tastes like is growing fast.

### This is the third wave, not the first

Britain has been here before, which is why the next three lessons are history.

1. **1860s to 1910.** Japanese art and design became a Victorian fashion. The [Japan-British Exhibition of 1910](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan%E2%80%93British_Exhibition) at White City drew over 8 million visitors.
2. **1970s to 1990s.** Japanese companies set up in Britain and a [resident community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_community_of_London) grew around them, with its own schools and shops. Yaohan Plaza, a Japanese shopping centre in north-west London, opened in 1993 at the peak. It was sold in 1999.
3. **1992 to now.** Japanese food and popular culture moved from that community to the general public.

### What this means if you look at it as a business

These points are my reading of the facts above, not a sourced claim.

1. **Demand has outrun authentic supply.** The mass market is "Japanese-inspired". A growing group of customers has now been to Japan and can tell the difference.
2. **Outbound travel is the bigger flow.** Services for Britons going to Japan, before, during and after the trip, address the larger and faster-growing side.
3. **London is not the whole market.** The main festival has expanded to Manchester, and most restaurants on the wider count are outside London.

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Inbound / outbound | Travel into a country / out of it. Britons visiting Japan are Japan's inbound and Britain's outbound |
| JNTO | Japan National Tourism Organization, which promotes travel to Japan |
| JETRO | Japan External Trade Organization, which promotes Japanese exports and investment |
| Golden Route | The standard first trip: Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka |
| Cool Japan | The Japanese government's policy of promoting its culture and content abroad |
| Grab-and-go | Pre-packed food sold from a chiller, the form most British sushi takes |

lessons.title: 1862 to 1910: Japonisme and the great exhibitions
lessons.body:
Victorian Britain did not discover Japan through Japanese companies. It bought Japan through a British diplomat's collection, a Regent Street shop, a handful of designers and importers, and a showman in Knightsbridge. Japan's government only took control of how it was sold in Britain at the very end of the period, with the 1910 exhibition at White City. That pattern, British intermediaries first and the Japanese state arriving later, is the same one lesson 1 found in today's restaurant market.

### The door opens: 1858 to 1862

Trade needed a treaty first. Lord Elgin signed the [Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Amity and Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Japanese_Treaty_of_Amity_and_Commerce) with the Tokugawa shogunate, the military government then ruling Japan, on 26 August 1858. Hakodate, Kanagawa and Nagasaki opened to British merchants on 1 July 1859. British traders could now buy Japanese goods at source.

The goods that came first were not chosen by Japan. They were chosen by British officials and merchants, for British taste.

### 1862: a diplomat's collection at South Kensington

The first large public showing of Japanese objects in Britain was at the London International Exhibition of 1862. Japan sent no official exhibits. The Japanese section was put together by Rutherford Alcock, Britain's first diplomatic representative in Japan, and by Captain F. Howard Vyse, the British consul at Kanagawa ([V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O130487)).

According to Japan's National Diet Library, it included lacquerware, swords, straw raincoats, lanterns and straw sandals ([NDL](https://ndl.go.jp/exposition/e/s1/1862-1.html)). An article on Oxford University Press's blog puts the section at more than 600 objects ([OUP](https://jvc.oup.com/?p=9661)). I did not find an official count to check this against.

A shogunate embassy of 38 people, led by Takeuchi Yasunori (竹内保徳), was in London and attended the opening on 1 May. Europeans praised the display. One member of the embassy, Fuchibe Tokuzō, wrote in his diary that it looked like old bric-a-brac and was shabby ([NDL](https://ndl.go.jp/exposition/e/s1/1862-1.html)). The embassy spent its time on the machinery halls, a dockyard and an arms factory.

That split is the first lesson of the period. The British were buying Japan as craft and exoticism. The Japanese visitors were shopping for industry.

### The shop: from Farmer & Rogers to Liberty

The route from exhibition to customer ran through Regent Street. In 1862 a 19-year-old, Arthur Lasenby Liberty, joined Farmer & Rogers, a shawl emporium there. The firm is believed to have bought much of the Japanese section after the exhibition and sold it through its Oriental Warehouse, which Liberty went on to manage ([OUP](https://jvc.oup.com/?p=9661)). Whistler, Rossetti, Albert Moore and William Morris are named as customers.

In 1875 Liberty set up on his own, with half a shop at 218a Regent Street, three staff and a £2,000 loan from his future father-in-law ([Wikipedia: Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_(department_store))). He sold ornaments, fabric and decorative objects, especially from Japan and the East. His "art fabrics" borrowed from the kimono's loose drape.

Liberty and his wife travelled to Japan in 1889, fourteen years after he opened. His shop was selling a British idea of Japan to British customers, and the idea was good enough to build a business on.

### The designers and the importers

The craze needed a name and a look. The French critic Philippe Burty is credited with coining "Japonisme" in the early 1870s for the Western fashion for Japanese art and design ([Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/art-terms/j/japonisme)). Tate names the painter James McNeill Whistler as the main channel of Japanese influence into British art, and the designer Christopher Dresser and the architect E. W. Godwin as the key figures in design. Their work became known as the Anglo-Japanese style ([OUP](https://jvc.oup.com/?p=9661)).

Dresser is the clearest case of a designer turning into a trader. In 1876 to 1877 he spent four months in Japan, representing the South Kensington Museum, and was asked by the Japanese government to write a report on trade with Europe ([Wikipedia: Dresser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Dresser)). Tiffany of New York commissioned him to buy a collection of Japanese goods while there. From 1879 to 1882 he and Charles Holme ran Dresser & Holme, wholesale importers of Oriental goods, from a warehouse at 7 Farringdon Road. Holme later travelled to Japan with the Libertys in 1889.

### Japan starts selling for itself

The Meiji (明治) government that followed the shogunate learned fast. Japan's first official appearance at a European exhibition was Paris in 1867 ([V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O130487)), and its first as the Meiji government was Vienna in 1873 ([NDL](https://ndl.go.jp/exposition/e/s1/1873-2.html)).

At Vienna an adviser, G. Wagener, argued that Japan should show finely made craft goods rather than machines that imitated Western ones. It worked. Thousands of fans sold out within a week, and a British trading company, Alexander Park, bought the Japanese garden buildings with their trees and stones. Afterwards the government set up Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha (起立工商会社), a company to sell Japanese crafts abroad, which signed a contract with the same British firm. The aim was foreign currency.

This is the point where Japan first acted as a seller in Europe rather than a source of goods.

### 1885: Japan as entertainment

The mass market came through showbusiness. On 10 January 1885 the Japanese Native Village opened at Humphreys' Hall in Knightsbridge ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Village,_Knightsbridge)). It was a private venture by Tannaker Buhicrosan. Around 100 Japanese craftspeople and performers lived and worked on site. Visitors paid a shilling, watched artisans at work, took tea served from lacquer trays and bought fans, toys and instruments in its shops ([Londonist](https://londonist.com/london/history/japanese-village-victorian-knightsbridge)).

About 250,000 people came in the first months. The Embassy of Japan says the first four months, Londonist says five ([Embassy of Japan](https://www.uk.emb-japan.go.jp/en/event/japanese_village.html)). Wikipedia reports over a million by February 1887. A fire on 2 May 1885 burned the hall down and killed a Japanese wood carver. It reopened that December and ran until June 1887.

The Japanese authorities did not cooperate. They worried it showed Japanese people as inferior to Westerners.

Gilbert and Sullivan's *The Mikado* opened at the Savoy Theatre on 14 March 1885 and ran for 672 performances ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mikado)). Gilbert had the idea before the village opened, but its residents coached his cast, and the first-night programme thanked them.

### 1910: the state takes the stage

The period closes with Japan presenting itself. The [Japan-British Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan%E2%80%93British_Exhibition) ran at White City from 14 May to 29 October 1910 and drew over 8 million visitors. About 2,271 Japanese exhibitors and almost 500 firms took part, and the Diet voted a large sum to pay for it.

The [Embassy of Japan](https://www.uk.emb-japan.go.jp/en/event/webmagazine/1910_exhibition.html) describes its purposes as celebrating the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902, promoting trade, and presenting Japan as a modern nation and an imperial power. It included displays from Taiwan and Korea, and "villages" of Ainu and Taiwanese indigenous people. British newspapers mostly praised it. In Japan it was widely judged a failure, partly because of those sideshows.

### Who sold Japan to Britain, 1862 to 1910

| Seller | Example | What they sold | How it reached customers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| British officials | Alcock, 1862 | Their own collections | Public exhibition |
| British retailers | Farmer & Rogers, Liberty | Crafts, fabrics, decorative objects | Regent Street shops |
| British designer-importers | Dresser & Holme | Wholesale Japanese goods and a style | Warehouse to trade buyers |
| Showmen | Japanese Native Village | An experience, plus souvenirs | Ticketed attraction |
| Japanese state | Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha, 1910 exhibition | Crafts, then a national image | Exhibitions and export agents |

### What this means if you look at it as a business

These points are my reading of the history above, not a sourced claim.

1. **Intermediaries capture the early value.** The people who made money from the first wave were the British who chose, framed and sold Japanese goods, not the makers. Lesson 1 found the same with Wagamama and YO! Sushi.
2. **Curation is the product.** Liberty sold a selection and a look more than any single object. Today's equivalent is the restaurant or shop that edits Japan for a British customer.
3. **Experience reaches the mass market first.** A shilling ticket to Knightsbridge reached far more people than Regent Street did. Events still do that job.
4. **Official Japan arrives late and with different goals.** In 1910 the state wanted prestige and alliance as much as sales. Expect the same mixed goals from Japan House and tourism bodies (lessons 13 and 16).

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Japonisme | French term from the early 1870s for the Western craze for Japanese art and design |
| Anglo-Japanese style | British furniture and decorative design using Japanese forms, linked to Godwin and Dresser |
| Treaty port | A Japanese port opened to foreign merchants by treaty, such as Kanagawa or Nagasaki from 1859 |
| Tokugawa shogunate | The military government that ruled Japan before the Meiji era and signed the first treaties |
| Meiji (明治) | The era and government that followed the shogunate and used exhibitions to promote Japan |
| Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha (起立工商会社) | Government-backed company set up after 1873 to sell Japanese crafts abroad |
| World's fair | A large international exhibition where countries showed goods to buyers and the public |

lessons.title: A huge vineyard, a small wine industry
lessons.body:
Turkey grows more grapes than almost any country, yet makes very little wine. Almost everything else about the industry follows from that gap, so it is the first thing to understand.

### The numbers

Turkey had about 395,000 hectares of vineyard in 2025, the sixth largest area in the world, according to [OIV figures](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/turkiye/). That is 5.6% of all the vineyard on earth. A few years ago it ranked fifth.

Very little of that fruit becomes wine. One widely quoted OIV figure says only [3% of the harvest](https://www.decanter.com/wine/turkey-wine-lands-on-the-rise-535193/) is used for winemaking. The [WSET](https://www.wsetglobal.com/knowledge-centre/blog/2023/june/13/exploring-the-wines-of-tuerkiye-turkey) puts wine grapes at around 15% of vineyard area. The two measure different things, but both say the same: wine is a small corner of Turkish grape growing.

For comparison, [Jancis Robinson's site](https://jancisrobinson.com/articles/young-turks-and-old-vines) puts the wine share at 96% in France and Spain. In Turkey the rest is eaten fresh or turned into raisins, molasses, vinegar and rakı. The most planted grape, Sultaniye, is the seedless grape sold elsewhere as sultanas.

The result is a wine industry of about 185 producers, by Decanter's count in 2024. [Falstaff](https://www.falstaff.com/nordics/regions-in-turkey) puts output at about 600,000 hectolitres a year, which is 60 million litres. It also puts consumption at under one litre per person a year.

### Why the gap exists

The WSET gives three historical reasons.

1. **Ottoman rule.** Only the non-Muslim population was permitted to produce and consume wine, so winemaking sat with Greek, Armenian and other minority communities.
2. **The 1923 population exchange.** When those communities left for Greece, much of the country's vineyard skill and winemaking knowledge left with them.
3. **The state monopoly.** From 1925, wine production and distribution were consolidated under the state, leaving little room for private investors.

Private producers did exist. Kavaklıdere, founded in Ankara in 1929, describes itself as the country's first private-sector wine producer. But for most of the twentieth century, wine was a bulk product with little attention to quality.

### The modern industry is about 30 years old

The turn came in the early 1990s. Doluca began making fine wines from international grapes, and Kavaklıdere began making wines from native grapes at about the same time. Decanter quotes the Turkish wine expert Levon Bağış calling these two moves the milestones of the modern story.

Since then the sector has grown quickly from a small base. The WSET says production has more than doubled since 2000 and consumption has nearly tripled. The growth has been driven by domestic investors and domestic drinkers, and exports remain low.

Most of the names you will meet are therefore young. Many boutique wineries were founded after 2000, often by people who made their money in another field.

### Where the wine comes from

The trade body Wines of Turkey divides the country into seven regions. Other sources draw the map differently, and the WSET credits the Aegean with nearer 30%, so treat the shares as rough.

| Region | Share of wine production | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aegean (İzmir, Denizli, Manisa) | 52.7% | The largest region; native and international grapes; the Urla route |
| Mid-Eastern Anatolia (Elazığ, Malatya, Tokat) | 14.7% | Home of Öküzgözü (red) and Narince (white) |
| Marmara, including Thrace | 13.6% | Close to Istanbul; many boutique estates |
| Mid-Southern Anatolia (Cappadocia) | 12.1% | Volcanic soils; home of Emir (white) |
| South-East Anatolia (Diyarbakır) | 3.4% | Home of Boğazkere (red) |
| Mid-Northern Anatolia (Ankara) | 3.3% | Home of Kalecik Karası (red) |
| Mediterranean | 0.2% | Very small |

Turkey has [no appellation system](https://www.winetraveler.com/?p=22827). Nothing like France's protected place names tells a buyer what a region guarantees. In practice people buy by producer name, which makes reputation the main asset a winery owns.

### Five grapes to know first

Turkey has recorded 1,435 grape varieties, and about 60 are used commercially for wine. Five native grapes carry most of the country's identity.

- **Öküzgözü** (red, from Elazığ): medium-bodied and fruity with soft tannins. The name means "eye of the bull".
- **Boğazkere** (red, from Diyarbakır): dark and very tannic. The name means "throat burner". It is often blended with Öküzgözü.
- **Kalecik Karası** (red, from near Ankara): lighter, crisp and low in tannin.
- **Narince** (white, from Tokat): the leading native white, often compared to Chardonnay.
- **Emir** (white, from Cappadocia): light, high in acidity, used for still and sparkling wine.

### The rules that shape the business

Three constraints come up in almost every conversation about Turkish wine. Later lessons take each in depth.

- **Promotion is banned.** A 2013 law prohibits advertising and promoting alcohol. Wineries cannot market in the ordinary sense.
- **Production is licensed.** A new producer needs both a facility permit and a production permit from the Tobacco and Alcohol Department of the agriculture ministry.
- **You must make your own wine.** Contract production, where one winery makes wine for another company's brand, has been banned since 2009. A brand cannot start without its own licensed facility.

### What this means if you look at it as a business

These three points are my reading of the facts above, not a sourced claim.

1. **Grapes are plentiful; good wine grapes are not.** A country full of table-grape vineyards does not make sourcing easy. Quality producers tend to plant their own or tie growers in closely.
2. **Selling is the hard part.** A small domestic market and a ban on promotion push wineries towards selling through visits, restaurants and personal reputation.
3. **Native grapes are the differentiator.** Turkey cannot out-compete established countries on Cabernet. Its own varieties are what nobody else has.

### Key terms

| Turkish | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| bağ | vineyard |
| bağ bozumu | grape harvest |
| şarap | wine |
| şaraphane | winery |
| bağ rotası / bağ yolu | vineyard route |
| yerli üzüm | native grape |

lessons.title: Ancient Anatolia to the Ottomans
lessons.body:
Wine in Anatolia is very old, but for most of the last 600 years the people who made it were not the people who ruled. Under the Ottomans, winemaking was the business of Greek, Armenian and other non-Muslim communities, while the state banned, tolerated and taxed it in turns. That arrangement explains both the late Ottoman export boom and the collapse that followed, which is where Lesson 3 picks up.

### Where the vine was tamed

Anatolia is one of the places where the wine grape (*Vitis vinifera*) was first domesticated. "Domesticated" means people selected wild vines and grew them as a crop. [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/wine/turkey-wine-lands-on-the-rise-535193/), citing a 2023 study in *Science*, names south-eastern Anatolia as one of two prime locations, with a date range of around 9,500 to 5,000 BCE.

Sources date this differently. The trade body [Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/) says winemaking in Anatolia goes back about 7,000 years and places domestication in the area shared by eastern Anatolia, Georgia and Armenia. The two are not in conflict: the *Science* range starts earlier and is about the grape itself, while the 7,000-year figure is about wine. This lesson uses the *Science* range for the grape and "at least 7,000 years" for wine.

### Hittites and Phrygians: wine for gods and kings

The Hittites ruled central Anatolia in the second millennium BCE. Wine was their main offering to the gods in royal rituals, and Hittite law protected vineyards, according to [Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/). [Wikipedia's summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine) adds that damaging a vineyard carried a fine. The Quirky Cork dates Hittite ritual winemaking to [as far back as 1600 BC](https://thequirkycork.com/five-surprising-things-turkish-wine/).

The Phrygians followed. Their best-known wine evidence comes from the tomb of King Midas at Gordion. Around 700 BCE, mourners shared a mixed drink of grape wine, barley beer and mead (fermented honey). Three bronze cauldrons held nearly 120 gallons of it. The archaeochemist Patrick McGovern's team identified the residues and published in *Nature* in 1999 ([Biblical Archaeology Society](https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/sidebar/the-death-of-midas-an-eternal-feast/)).

### Greeks and Romans: the Aegean as an export coast

On the Aegean coast, wine became a traded product. By the 6th century BCE, wine was shipped to France and Italy from Tabae (today's Tavas), Klazomenai (today's Urla) and Ainos (today's Enez), according to [Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/). The same source says the Misket grape became known in Europe as Muscat, and that Homer's *Iliad* mentions Pramnian wine made from a grape of Smyrna (İzmir).

Several of these places are wine names again. Urla is now one of the best-known modern routes, as Lesson 1 noted.

### Byzantium: monastery wine for the capital

The Byzantine Empire, ruled from Constantinople (Istanbul), kept wine central to church and city life. A useful example is Ganos, a large monastery at today's Gaziköy near Tekirdağ, on the Sea of Marmara. A [nautical archaeology study](https://nautarch.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Ganos_Wine.pdf) describes how Ganos and nearby villages made their own wine jars (amphorae) in kilns, held vineyards on Marmara Island, and shipped wine largely to Constantinople in the 11th century and probably the 12th. Ganos amphorae have been found from Egypt to Kiev and Sweden.

This was an integrated business: vineyards, packaging, a harbour and probably its own ships, all under one owner. Tekirdağ wineries still use the Ganos name.

### The Ottoman system: who could make wine

The Ottoman Empire lasted from 1299 to 1923, the dates [Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/) and the economist [Durmuş Özdemir](https://ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/164655/files/AAWE_WP143.pdf) use. Islamic law forbids alcohol, so the empire split the trade by religion.

- **Producers and traders** were almost entirely non-Muslim (*gayrimüslim*): Rum (Greek Orthodox), Armenians, Syriacs and Jews ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine)).
- **Growers** could be Muslim. Many Muslims grew grapes and sold them to Greek and Armenian winemakers ([The Quirky Cork](https://thequirkycork.com/five-surprising-things-turkish-wine/)).
- **Drinkers** crossed the line. Wine bars, usually in Christian neighbourhoods, were also used by Muslims ([Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/)).

Sultans banned alcohol from time to time, with heavy penalties. Each ban was lifted, because wine sales taxes were an important income for the treasury ([Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/); [Özdemir](https://ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/164655/files/AAWE_WP143.pdf)). Vineyards were not uprooted during bans. Grapes went to other uses, so wine came back quickly.

The tax itself shows the compromise. The alcohol tax, *müskirat resmi*, was introduced in the 17th century for non-Muslims and was collected by tax farming. Tax farming means the state sold the right to collect a tax to a private contractor; here the contractors were non-Muslims, so Muslim officials stayed out of the alcohol trade. In the 19th-century reform era (*Tanzimat*) the rate was simplified to 20%, cut to 10% in 1861 and then raised to 15% ([Wikipedia: Müskirat resmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCskirat_resmi)). Smyrna (İzmir) was an active export port for wine and vine products by the 17th century ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine)).

### Phylloxera: Europe's disaster, Anatolia's boom

Phylloxera is a tiny aphid-like insect from North America that kills vines by feeding on their roots. In the late 19th century it devastated Europe's vineyards. France was short of wine, and Ottoman producers filled the gap.

1. **The boom.** Production reached record levels in the second half of the 19th century, and exports rose to 340 million litres in 1904, according to [Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/). I found this figure in only one source; [The Quirky Cork](https://thequirkycork.com/five-surprising-things-turkish-wine/) says only "millions of litres". Treat 340 million litres as the trade body's claim. For scale, it is more than five times the whole of today's output of about 60 million litres (Lesson 1).
2. **The pest arrives.** The Ottoman state issued its first anti-phylloxera regulation in 1880. Traces appeared on the Anatolian side of Istanbul in 1885, the state admitted the outbreak in 1886, and it spread to Aydın province, the main grape area ([Ege Journal of Historical Research abstract](https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/egetid/article/185956)).
3. **The fix.** As in France, the long-term answer was grafting local varieties onto American rootstocks, which resist the insect. The state set up nurseries in Istanbul, İzmir, Urla and Manisa, gave seedlings free to growers, and offered tithe (*öşür*) exemptions and cheap Ziraat Bankası loans to those who replanted (same source).

### War and exchange: the end of the old industry

Wars from World War I to the War of Independence hit production, especially in Thrace and the Aegean ([Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/wine-histroy-in-anatolia/)). Then the 1923 population exchange (*mübadele*) between Greece and Turkey removed most of the Greek Orthodox community. [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/wine/turkey-wine-lands-on-the-rise-535193/) says Armenian and Greek communities, the main producers, were forced to leave, and vineyards and wineries were abandoned. About 379,000 exchangees arrived in Turkey from Greece between 1923 and 1933 ([Hürriyet Daily News](https://hurriyetdailynews.com/turkish-greek-population-swap-marks-102nd-year-205262)), but they did not bring an equivalent wine trade with them.

The vineyards largely stayed. What left was the know-how, the cellars and the buyers who had turned grapes into wine. That is why the new Republic had to rebuild wine almost from scratch.

### What this means if you look at it as a business

This section is my reading of the history above, not a sourced claim.

- **The grape-wine gap is old.** Muslim growers selling grapes, with others doing the winemaking, is the same split Lesson 1 described: a huge vineyard, a small wine industry. Wine skills were held by a minority and could leave in a single decade.
- **Regulation by tolerance is a pattern.** The Ottoman state banned, then taxed. Today's mix of high tax, licensing and a promotion ban is a modern version: wine is permitted, earns revenue and is kept out of sight.
- **Export booms can be borrowed.** The 1900s exports depended on France's crisis, not on Anatolian brands. When France replanted, the advantage went.
- **History is a marketing asset.** With advertising banned, producers lean on place names such as Urla, Ganos and Misket, and on stories of thousands of years of winemaking. The facts support a strong story, but the exact dates vary by source, so use them with care.

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *Vitis vinifera* | The Eurasian wine-grape species; almost all wine is made from it |
| domestication | Selecting wild plants and growing them as a crop |
| amfora (amphora) | Clay transport jar used for wine in the ancient and Byzantine world |
| gayrimüslim | Non-Muslim; in Ottoman usage, the Christian and Jewish subjects who made wine |
| müskirat resmi | Ottoman tax on alcoholic drinks |
| Rum | Greek Orthodox Christians of the Ottoman Empire, major winemakers until 1923 |
| filoksera (phylloxera) | Root-feeding insect from North America that destroyed European vineyards |
| mübadele | The 1923 Greek–Turkish population exchange |

Non-Muslim communities such as Greek Orthodox, Armenians, Syriacs and Jews
State-run cellars attached to the treasury
Foreign merchants from France and Italy

lessons.title: The Republic, Atatürk and the state monopoly
lessons.body:
The young Republic first banned alcohol, then turned it into a state revenue business. Spirits became a state monopoly, while wine stayed legally open to private makers. In practice the state was the biggest winemaker and controlled imports, so for about 75 years a handful of private houses grew up in its shadow. The monopoly's law from 1942 is still the legal base of today's alcohol rules.

### First, prohibition (1920–1926)

The new Ankara assembly's early instinct was to ban drink. A bill from the Trabzon deputy Ali Şükrü Bey, the *Men-i Müskirat Kanunu* (law banning intoxicants), passed in September 1920. It banned production, import, sale and consumption, according to a [history thesis by Yavuz Saç at İstanbul Bilgi University](https://openaccess.bilgi.edu.tr/bitstreams/fdfcf40c-aa17-4fec-b2d1-6e803896ef76/download). The vote was razor thin. Saç gives 72 to 71; a [Duvar English column](https://www.duvarenglish.com/turkish-republics-test-with-alcohol-in-its-second-century-article-63425) gives a 71–71 tie. I use the thesis, because it works from archival records.

The ban did not work. Illicit production went on, contraband arrived from the Greek islands and Bulgaria, and the state collected no tax (Saç). It was unwound in two steps:

1. **9 April 1924:** the assembly allowed licensed production, by 94 votes to 35.
2. **22 March 1926:** the ban was repealed completely.

Saç concludes that the main reason for lifting the ban was revenue. The state wanted to tax drink, and soon to make it.

### Building the monopoly

A **monopoly** (*inhisar*, later *tekel*) means only the state, or a firm it appoints, may produce or sell a product. The Republic inherited monopolies from the Ottoman debt administration and took them over step by step.

| Year | Step | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1925 | The tobacco Régie is nationalised | [Wikipedia: Tekel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekel) |
| 1926 | A new alcohol administration is set up; monopoly rights go to a company formed by İş Bankası and a Polish firm | [Duvar](https://www.duvarenglish.com/turkish-republics-test-with-alcohol-in-its-second-century-article-63425); [Saç](https://openaccess.bilgi.edu.tr/bitstreams/fdfcf40c-aa17-4fec-b2d1-6e803896ef76/download) |
| 1930 | Policy turns to *devletçilik* (statism); the state takes monopolies back from private firms | [Çağdaş Türkiye Tarihi Araştırmaları Dergisi](https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/pub/cttad/article/266950) |
| 1932 | A General Directorate of Monopolies is founded | [Wikipedia: Tekel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekel) |
| 1942 | Law No. 4250, the spirits monopoly law (*İspirto ve İspirtolu İçkiler İnhisarı Kanunu*), is adopted on 8 June | [Alomaliye: Law 4250](https://alomaliye.com/1942/06/12/4250-sayili-ispirto-ve-ispirtolu-ickiler-inhisari-kanunu/) |

The same journal article notes that monopoly income became a major part of the budget during the Second World War. That is the key to the whole period: alcohol was a fiscal tool first and an industry second.

### Was wine inside the monopoly?

Sources disagree. The [WSET](https://www.wsetglobal.com/knowledge-centre/blog/2023/june/13/exploring-the-wines-of-tuerkiye-turkey) says wine production and distribution were "consolidated under the state monopoly" from 1925. The economist [Durmuş Özdemir](https://ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/164655/files/AAWE_WP143.pdf) says that for about 70 years all alcoholic drinks *except wine* were produced only by the state monopoly. The current text of [Law 4250](https://alomaliye.com/1942/06/12/4250-sayili-ispirto-ve-ispirtolu-ickiler-inhisari-kanunu/) explicitly frees beer and wine from the monopoly, though that wording dates from a 2001 rewrite.

I follow Özdemir. Private wineries were founded and run throughout the period, which a full legal monopoly would not have allowed. The WSET's point still holds in practice: the state was the dominant producer, and it controlled imports and much of the trade. Wine paid a per-litre tax instead, 10 kuruş a litre after 1926 with a surcharge above 12% alcohol, cut to a flat 5 kuruş in 1931 (Saç).

### The state as winemaker

The state did not just tax wine; it made it. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine) says Atatürk ordered a state winery at Tekirdağ in 1925. Saç dates the first state-owned wine factory to 1930, in the Mürefte–Şarköy area. Both are on the Tekirdağ coast, so the gap may be the difference between an order and an opening, but I could not confirm that.

Under the monopoly body later called Tekel, the network grew. The Elazığ winery was founded in 1942, and Tekel's best-known wine was the red Buzbağ ([Wine with Seth](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/kayra-turkeys-iconic-cross-regional-powerhouse/)). By the end, Tekel had wine factories in Tekirdağ, Elazığ, Ürgüp and Kırıkkale ([Capital](https://www.capital.com.tr/sektorler/gida/kadeh-kadeh-yatirim-keyfi)).

The elite also gave wine a cultural role. By the end of the 1920s, drinking wine at state receptions had become fashionable and was seen as a sign of Western values (Saç). Saç notes that Atatürk drank but does not describe a direct policy role for him in wine.

### The first private houses

Private wine was small but persistent. These are the founding dates the sources give.

| Winery | Founded | Where | Origin story |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Doluca | 1926 | Mürefte, Thrace | Nihat Kutman, trained at Geisenheim in Germany. His father bought abandoned Mürefte wineries after the 1923 population exchange, paying over eight years ([Wine with Seth](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/doluca-turkeys-second-largest-winery-modern-wine-pioneer/); Saç) |
| Kavaklıdere | 1929 | Ankara | Founded by Cenap And ([Bilkent project](https://repository.bilkent.edu.tr/items/f93c77a3-5d2e-4d94-9f1b-2bd026c3699e/full)); Saç credits the children of Tunalı Hilmi, a deputy who opposed prohibition |
| Sevilen | 1942 | İzmir | [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine) |
| Diren | 1958 | Tokat | [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine) |

Lesson 1 quoted Kavaklıdere calling itself the first private-sector wine producer, yet Doluca's date is earlier. The claims depend on what counts as the start, so treat "first" as marketing on both sides.

Doluca shows how the population exchange (*mübadele*, Lesson 2) fed the new industry. Saç says private makers flourished in Mürefte partly because the departed Greek owners left equipment and a trained workforce behind. Kutman also brought international grapes to Turkey in the 1930s and 1940s ([Wine with Seth](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/doluca-turkeys-second-largest-winery-modern-wine-pioneer/)).

### How the monopoly ended

The structure lasted into this century. Until June 2003, wine imports went only through Tekel, and distributors could sell imported wine only to tourism-licensed hotels and restaurants ([Capital](https://www.capital.com.tr/sektorler/gida/kadeh-kadeh-yatirim-keyfi)). Özdemir counts only 12 wine producers in 2000.

Then came privatisation (*özelleştirme*):

1. **2001–2002:** Article 1 of Law 4250 was rewritten in 2001 (Law 4619). A new market regulator, TAPDK, was set up under Law 4733 to license producers, importers and sellers; its production by-law dates from 2002 ([Alomaliye](https://alomaliye.com/1942/06/12/4250-sayili-ispirto-ve-ispirtolu-ickiler-inhisari-kanunu/); [EU screening document](https://www.ab.gov.tr/files/tarama/tarama_files/11/SC11DET_25a_Wine.pdf)).
2. **February 2004:** Tekel's drinks business, renamed Mey İçki, was sold for $292 million to a consortium of Nurol, Limak, Özaltın and Tütsab ([Limak, quoting the press](https://www.limak.com.tr/news-and-press/limak-in-the-press/2006-en/texas-pacific-buys-turkish-raki-maker-mey-for-900-mln)).
3. **2006:** Texas Pacific Group bought 90% of Mey at a $900 million valuation (same source). [Jancis Robinson's site](https://jancisrobinson.com/ja/node/201534) dates the TPG purchase to 2004; I use the contemporary report.

Tekel's wineries became Kayra, part of Mey, which now sits in Diageo's portfolio ([Wine with Seth](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/kayra-turkeys-iconic-cross-regional-powerhouse/), which dates Kayra's privatisation to 2005). Just after the sale, Capital put Kavaklıdere at about 30% of the market, Doluca at 25% and Tekel at about 20%.

### What this means if you look at it as a business

This is my reading of the history, not a sourced claim.

- **Today's rules sit on a fiscal law.** Law 4250 was written to protect a state revenue stream. The 2013 promotion ban and the 2026 sponsorship rules were added to that same law, which helps explain why wine is regulated like a tax product.
- **The big two are incumbents from a protected market.** Doluca and Kavaklıdere grew for decades with the state as their only large rival and imports kept out. Their scale, distribution reach and brand recognition date from that era.
- **Kayra is the state's old asset base.** A buyer of Kayra inherited vineyards, wineries and a national brand that no start-up could build quickly.
- **The boutique era needed the monopoly gone.** Twelve producers in 2000 against about 185 today (Lesson 1) shows how much opened up once imports and distribution were freed.

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Men-i Müskirat Kanunu | The 1920 law banning alcohol; repealed in 1926 |
| inhisar | Monopoly (Ottoman and early Republican word) |
| Tekel | "Single hand": the state tobacco and alcohol monopoly, and its later name |
| devletçilik | Statism: the 1930s policy of the state running key industries |
| Law 4250 | The 1942 spirits monopoly law; still the base of Turkish alcohol rules |
| TAPDK | The alcohol and tobacco market regulator set up under Law 4733 |
| özelleştirme | Privatisation |
| Mey İçki | The company formed from Tekel's drinks business; owner of Kayra |

options: Atatürk personally ordered its repeal
The state wanted tax revenue from drink, and soon to produce it
European governments demanded it in the Lausanne treaty
Wine exports had collapsed and needed rescuing
quiz.q: Why, according to the lesson's main historical source, did the Republic lift its 1920 alcohol ban?
quiz.why: Saç concludes the main motive was revenue: the ban created smuggling and no tax. Atatürk is often linked with wine, but the thesis does not describe a direct policy role for him in the repeal.

options: Wine was banned for private producers until 2004
Wine was fully free; the state made no wine
Wine was the only drink the monopoly covered
Private wine production was legal, but the state was the biggest producer and controlled imports
quiz.q: Which statement best describes wine's position under the state monopoly system?
quiz.why: Private wineries like Doluca and Kavaklıdere operated throughout, so wine was not fully monopolised (Özdemir), yet Tekel ran several wineries and handled all imports until 2003. The WSET's 'consolidated under the state' is the tempting answer but describes practical dominance, not a legal ban.

options: Its later amendments carry the advertising ban, sales hours and sponsorship rules
It set up the appellation system for Turkish regions
It fixed the per-litre wine tax that is still charged
It guarantees state purchase of surplus grapes
quiz.q: Why does Law No. 4250 of 1942 still matter to a Turkish winery today?
quiz.why: The 2013 promotion ban and the 2026 sponsorship and brand rules were written into Law 4250, the old monopoly law. Turkey has no appellation system, and the 1920s per-litre wine tax is long gone.

options: It was a spin-off of a Tekel winery
It was founded by a foreign wine company
It grew from wineries and skilled workers left behind after the 1923 population exchange
It started as a rakı distillery and moved into wine in the 1990s
quiz.q: What does Doluca's origin story show about how the private industry began?
quiz.why: Kutman's father bought abandoned Mürefte wineries after the exchange, and Saç says the equipment and trained workforce left behind helped private makers there. Doluca was never part of Tekel; Kayra is the ex-Tekel business.

options: The 1931 cut in the wine tax to 5 kuruş a litre
The end of Tekel's control of imports and distribution and its privatisation in 2003–2004
The founding of the General Directorate of Monopolies in 1932
The 1942 founding of Sevilen in İzmir
quiz.q: Which change most directly opened the market to the boutique wineries of the 2000s?
quiz.why: Only 12 producers existed in 2000; after imports and distribution were freed and Tekel's drinks arm was sold as Mey, the producer count rose sharply. The 1931 tax cut is real but came while the monopoly system was being built, not dismantled.

news.headline: 後継者難倒産、年度上半期として過去最多の263件。
news.body: 東京商工リサーチによると、4〜9月の後継者難倒産は前年同期比23.4%増。代表者の死亡（120件）と体調不良（105件）で85.5%を占め、資本金1千万円未満が68.4%でした。
news.why: 2年続いた減少が止まり、再び増加に転じました。TSR自身も、事業継続か譲渡か廃業かを経営者が早く決断する必要があると結論づけています。

news.headline: 1〜6月の後継者難倒産も過去最多の264件。
news.body: 96.2%が破産でした。
news.why: 倒産した後に再建される会社はほとんどありません。引き継ぐ機会があるのは倒産の前です。

news.headline: 佐嘉酒造が全面リニューアルを完了。
news.body: 福岡の地域みらいグループ傘下で330年余りの歴史を持つ佐嘉酒造が、3年がかりで5棟を新築しました。
news.why: 古い蔵を引き継いだ地域企業が、維持にとどまらず大きく投資した例です。

news.headline: ベストアメニティが老舗酒蔵「花の露」を承継。
news.body: 食品会社のベストアメニティが福岡の老舗酒蔵を承継したと報じられました（有料記事のため見出しのみ確認）。
news.why: 食品・飲料の会社が酒蔵の買い手として定着しつつあります。

news.headline: 経産省の研究会が伝統的工芸品を取り上げる。
news.body: エンタメ・クリエイティブ政策研究会が、伝統的工芸品をアニメやファッション、デザインと並ぶ産業として位置づけました。
news.why: 政策の重心が、工芸の保存から、他の日本発コンテンツと組み合わせた海外展開へ移りつつあります。

news.headline: 帝国データバンクの集計で、2026年度上半期の後継者難倒産が296件となり、上半期として過去最多になりました。
news.body: 前年同期の264件から12.1%増で、集計を始めた2013年度以降で最多です。同社は通年で600件前後になると見込んでいます。業歴100年以上の老舗の倒産も88件（前年同期比23.9%増）でした。
news.why: 同じ期間を東京商工リサーチは263件と集計しており、調査会社によって数字が違います。どちらも増加という方向は一致しています。

news.headline: 業歴100年超の老舗企業の倒産が、1〜8月で112件となり、過去最多のペースで推移しています。
news.body: これまでの最多は2024年の146件で、2026年は年間160件を上回るペースです。業種別では製造業34件、卸売業24件、小売業22件で、後継者難や物価高が背景とされています。
news.why: 老舗は家の仕組みで長く続いてきた会社ですが、承継と収益の両方の圧力で退出が増えています。

news.headline: 和菓子店の倒産が1〜9月で22件となり、過去最多だった2025年を上回るペースです。
news.body: 2020年以降の和菓子店の倒産138件のうち、業歴100年以上が24件（17.4%）でした。原材料高に加え、菓子職人の高齢化で技術の承継が難しくなり、生産量を保てない店も出ています。
news.why: 技能を持つ職人の引退が事業の継続を左右する点で、酒蔵や伝統工芸と同じ構造を持つ業種です。

news.headline: 東京商工リサーチが、法人版事業承継税制の活用状況と特例承継計画の提出期限延長をまとめました。
news.body: 特例承継計画の提出は2023年度の5,546件から2025年度は2,264件に減り、提出期限は2026年3月末から2027年9月30日に延びました。一方、特例の適用を受ける贈与・相続の期限は2027年12月31日のままです。1〜8月の後継者難倒産は355件で前年同期比17.1%増でした。
news.why: 相続税・贈与税の納税猶予が全額になる特例の期限が近づいており、株式の承継を考える会社には時間の制約になります。税金は免除ではなく猶予で、取り消されれば利子税と合わせて納める必要がある点も押さえておくべきです。

news.headline: 非上場株の相続評価の見直しについて、知っている企業は36.6%にとどまるという東京商工リサーチの調査が出ました。
news.body: 10月1〜8日に5,257社が回答しました。見直しを知る企業のうち56.2%が評価額は「上昇しそう」と答え、中小企業では57.1%でした。国税庁は2026年4月から有識者会議を開いており、経済産業省・中小企業庁は9月16日に慎重な検証を求める意見を出しています。
news.why: 自社株の評価が上がれば、親族への承継で相続税・贈与税の負担が増えます。承継の費用と時期を左右する論点として、第7回（お金の問題）にも関わります。

news.headline: Endo Kazutoshi due to open a 10-seat omakase restaurant in Chelsea.
news.body: Endo Chelsea has a listening bar upstairs. His White City restaurant remains closed after a fire.
news.why: The top end of Japanese dining in London is Japanese-led and still expanding. His group also plans a second Sumi in Marylebone this year.

news.headline: Nakimushi opens in a three-storey Notting Hill townhouse.
news.body: It has ramen downstairs and a broader Japanese menu above, and comes from the team behind Dorian.
news.why: British restaurateurs keep moving into Japanese formats, here by combining two successful pop-ups.

news.headline: The BBC reports a Japan travel craze among young Britons.
news.body: The report put it down to social media and the weak yen.
news.why: The boom is now mainstream news, which usually means the early-adopter phase is over.

news.headline: Hyper Japan runs at Olympia London.
news.body: Last year's festival drew 53,000 visitors.
news.why: This year's attendance is the figure to look for.

news.headline: VisitBritain forecasts 276,000 visits from Japan this year, up 18%.
news.body: It hosted Japanese tour operators around England.
news.why: The reverse flow is recovering, but from a much lower base than the outbound one.

news.headline: Japan's tourism agency appoints FINN Partners for UK marketing.
news.body: The agency will run its UK public relations and marketing.
news.why: The brief is to push repeat visitors to lesser-known regions, which is where new travel products will be wanted.

news.headline: Wagamama starts taking table bookings for the first time in its 34-year history.
news.body: The walk-in-only chain now accepts same-day and advance bookings for groups of any size through OpenTable, its website and app; groups of 20 or more book by phone. The company says the change followed a trial and guest requests, and is pushing it with a festive set menu at £23 for two courses.
news.why: The UK's largest Japanese-inspired chain is giving up a format rule it has kept since 1992, a sign that casual dining now competes on convenience and occasion bookings, not just on queue-and-eat.

news.headline: Zadie's, billed as Manchester's first Itameshi (Japanese-Italian) restaurant, opens at Medlock Square in East Manchester.
news.body: The venue has 258 covers plus 30 counter seats and was developed with Gorgeous Group; the head chef previously worked at Zuma and Lucky Cat. It sits in a £300m hospitality development in East Manchester.
news.why: Large-format, Japanese-fusion dining is spreading beyond London, here into a large new leisure development rather than a high street.

news.headline: JNTO figures show British visits to Japan flat in August and up only 5.8% for the year so far.
news.body: Japan recorded 36,600 UK arrivals in August 2026, down 0.2% on August 2025, and 364,800 for January to August, up 5.8%. Total arrivals to Japan fell 9.6% in August, mainly because visitors from China dropped 59%.
news.why: After 22% growth in 2025, the UK market is slowing sharply, which matters for anyone planning capacity in Japan travel on last year's trend.

news.headline: Harvest season promoted across the vineyard routes.
news.body: Routes from Cappadocia and Çal to Urla and the newer Lidya Antik route ran harvest events, with travel agencies offering harvest tours.
news.why: Visits are one of the few legal ways for a winery to meet customers. The routes are growing in number.

news.headline: A leading Turkish wine writer says she no longer knows what she may post.
news.body: The writer behind The Quirky Cork said she is unsure whether branded photos or tasting notes are still allowed.
news.why: Bloggers and Instagram accounts were how people learned about new Turkish wines. That channel is now uncertain.

news.headline: An actor is fined for an alcohol brand in his personal posts.
news.body: Yiğit Dören was fined 82,244 lira after an alcohol brand appeared in his personal social media posts. He has appealed.
news.why: It shows personal accounts can be penalised, not only companies. The 2026 range for promotion offences is 103,207 to 4,130,222 lira. The court's decision on his appeal is the thing to watch.

news.headline: Parliament bars alcohol producers from sponsoring events under their brand.
news.body: The law stops producers, importers and marketers supporting any event with their brand, logo or company name, and restricts logos inside and outside business premises. The parts covering broadcasts and social media took effect on 20 June.
news.why: It closes most of the indirect routes wineries used after the 2013 ban, such as sponsored dinners and events.

news.headline: DNA testing shows the rare grape Kolorko is Hungary's Furmint.
news.body: Testing by the Paşaeli winery and the grape geneticist José Vouillamoz identified the Marmara grape Kolorko as Furmint. The same work matched Çal Karası to Crete's Liatiko.
news.why: The native-grape story is now being checked by science. Some "Turkish" grapes turn out to be shared with neighbours.

news.headline: The special consumption tax on wine rises 7.95%.
news.body: The fixed tax (ÖTV) on wine went from 56.87 to 61.39 lira.
news.why: The tax is updated every January and July in line with producer prices, so shelf prices rise on a fixed timetable.

news.headline: Turkey's national viticulture symposium met in Tekirdağ, with native grapes and heat stress high on the agenda.
news.body: The 11th Turkish Viticulture and Technologies Symposium, hosted by the Tekirdağ Viticulture Research Institute with guests from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Bulgaria, heard papers on Öküzgözü from five Elazığ sites, Papazkarası wine yeasts, Kalecik Karası clones and protecting grapes from sunburn. A researcher from the institute said two Thracian producers are close to releasing wine from the revived Karamenüş grape; the next symposium is in Diyarbakır in 2030.
news.why: It shows where state-backed grape research is heading: native varieties, local yeasts and adapting vineyards to heat. A speaker also named the lack of wine-tourism policy as the main obstacle to that income stream.

news.headline: The agriculture minister forecast a 2026 grape crop of about 3.85 million tonnes, up from about 2.5 million in 2025.
news.body: Speaking at a harvest event in Kalecik, Ankara, İbrahim Yumaklı called 2026 the wettest year in 66 years. TÜİK's first crop estimate in May had already pointed to a 53% rise in grape production.
news.why: After the poor 2025 crop, a large harvest should ease grape supply and prices for wineries that buy fruit. Most of the crop is table and drying grapes, so the effect on wine grapes specifically is not stated.
